report.source_text: An open surgical exploration and washout of the wrist was carried out through a dorsal approach. Three millilitres of purulent and gelatinous tissue was drained from the carpal joint. The intraoperative appearance remained consistent with deep infection, and so infection remained the most likely diagnosis. Tissue samples were obtained for microbiological culture and sensitivities along with concurrent histological and cytological samples, in line with departmental policy.

clinician.final_diagnosis: invasive moderate to focally poorly differentiated basaloid squamous cell carcinoma with focal keratinisation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 54-year-old male smoker presented with left wrist ulnar border tenderness and swelling, which he attributed to an unprovoked dog bite 4 weeks prior. Initial investigations showed raised inflammatory markers and a normal wrist X-ray. He was treated with antimicrobial therapy with initial improvement, but symptoms recurred after cessation of antibiotics, prompting a second course of community-based antibiotics. At 8 weeks post-bite, repeat imaging revealed almost complete resorption of the hamate bone on X-ray, and MRI demonstrated a 30 x 21 mm inflammatory mass centered on the hamate with extensive marrow abnormality. Open surgical exploration and washout via dorsal approach was performed, draining 3 mL of purulent and gelatinous tissue from the carpal joint. Tissue samples obtained during surgery were sent for microbiological culture and histopathological analysis. Microbiological cultures did not isolate any organisms. Histopathology revealed fragments of fibroconnective tissue heavily infiltrated by invasive moderate to focally poorly differentiated basaloid squamous cell carcinoma with focal keratinisation, establishing the definitive diagnosis.
